title: Tomorrow we swim
title_target: Αύριο θα κολυμπήσουμε — Ahv-ree-oh thah koh-leem-bee-soo-meh
goal: Talk about what hasn't happened yet with one small word — and choose between two future forms that English "will" doesn't tell apart.
bekal: choose between the one-time and the repeated form
use θα ήθελα for polite requests

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — Saturday plans
dialogs.intro: Nikos and Ana make plans. Notice the two future forms side by side in lines three and eight: one for a single action, one for an action that goes on for a long time.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I'm going to the sea. Will you come?
lines.literal: will — I-go — to-the — sea. will — you-come?

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: I'd like to, but tomorrow I'm working all day.
lines.literal: will — I-want, but — will — I-work (ongoing) — all — the — day.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: On Saturday I'm free. We'll go together.
lines.literal: the — Saturday — will — I-am — free. will — we-go — together.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.literal: and — I — will — I-bring — water — and — fruits.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: And in the evening we'll eat at a taverna by the port.
lines.literal: and — the — evening — will — we-eat (once) — in — a — taverna — at-the — port.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: Me neither. I'll call you on Friday.
lines.literal: and — I. will — to-you — I-call (once) — the — Friday.

notes: **The Greek future needs just one word: θα.** It goes before the verb and never changes. That's simpler than French or Spanish, which have special future endings, and as easy as English *will*.

⚠️ **But you have to choose the verb form, and English won't help you here.** *Θα **πάω*** = I'll go (once, one trip). *Θα **πηγαίνω*** = I'll keep going, again and again, or for a long time. English "will" doesn't separate the two, so you have to make this choice consciously every time.

**The one-time form is the same as the form after να** from unit 12: θα πάω, θα φάω, θα πιω, θα δω, θα έρθω, θα πάρω, θα αγοράσω, θα μιλήσω. If you've learned it for να and for the past, you've learned it for the future too.

**The repeated form is just the ordinary everyday form**: θα δουλεύω, θα κολυμπάμε, θα μένω, θα διαβάζω. It's for activities that fill a stretch of time (*θα δουλεύω όλη μέρα*) or that repeat (*κάθε μέρα θα πηγαίνω στη δουλειά*).

**A rule of thumb that settles nine cases out of ten:** with **όλη / όλο** (all, whole), **κάθε** (every), **συνέχεια** (constantly), use the repeated form. Otherwise, use the one-time form. If you get it wrong, you'll still be understood — it just sounds slightly off.
**Negating: δεν goes before θα**, not after it. *Δεν θα πάω αύριο.* — I won't go tomorrow. In fast speech δεν θα often melts into *δε θα*.

**Θα ήθελα = "I would like"**, the politest request form. It's really a conditional, not a future, but it's used exactly like *I would like*. Its cousins: **Θα μπορούσα;** ("could I…?") and **Θα μπορούσες να…;** ("could you…?").

**Θα is also used for guessing, not just the future.** *Πού είναι ο Νίκος; — Θα είναι στο σπίτι.* — "Where's Nikos? — He'll be at home." ⚠️ This use often confuses beginners: the sentence looks future but is about now — just like English "that'll be the mailman".

**Ανυπομονώ** (*ah-nee-poh-moh-NOH*) literally "I'm impatient", is used exactly like *I can't wait*. It's the negative of υπομονή (patience) — a word you'll hear a lot: **Υπομονή!** means "be patient".

grammars.title: Two futures, one lead-in word
body: Compare the pairs below. English "will" blurs the difference, so read the translations slowly.
after: **Είμαι and έχω don't have two forms** — they always use the ordinary one: **θα είμαι**, **θα έχω**, **θα είναι**, **θα έχουμε**. The two most important verbs are the easiest again.
⚠️ When in doubt, use the **one-time form**. It's right most often, and even when it misses, no Greek speaker will misunderstand you.

grammars.title: Planning and offering
body: Ready-made sentences for making plans, all built on θα.

head: Greek
Say it
Meaning
rows: See you! *(literally: we'll talk about it)*

after: **Θα τα πούμε!** is the most typically Greek goodbye after Γεια σου — literally "we'll talk about it", meaning "see you around". Its cousin **Τα λέμε!** is just as casual.

blocks.title: Greek wishes for things to come
items: **Καλή συνέχεια!** — enjoy the rest · **Καλό ταξίδι!** — have a good trip · **Καλή επιτυχία!** — good luck · **Καλό μήνα!** — happy new month, said on the first of every month.
**Καλή εβδομάδα!** — have a good week, said every Monday morning. ⚠️ Greeks have a wish for almost every beginning, and saying it before the other person does is always warmly received.

**Στην υγειά μας!** (*steen ee-YAH mahs*) — cheers, literally "to our health". The short form is **Γεια μας!** — which sounds exactly like the "hello" you learned in unit 1, because it's the same word.
**Υπομονή!** — be patient. What Greeks will tell you when you complain about lines, bureaucracy, or the Greek language itself.
